title: Netflix Data Analysis
text:
Netflix Media with Murder
For this graph, I wanted to look at the content ratings of movies and TV shows on Netflix that mention murder or killing in their descriptions. I filtered the data to include descriptions containing the words “murder,” “kill,” or “killed.” I then made a bar graph to compare how many movies and TV shows fall into each rating category. I was interested in seeing whether media that mentions murder tends to have more mature ratings and whether there is a difference between movies and TV shows.


Show Code
netflix_titles <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-04-20/netflix_titles.csv')
netflix_titles <- netflix_titles|>
  mutate(rating_fct = fct_relevel(factor(rating),  "G", "TV-Y", "TV-G", "TV-Y7", "TV-Y7-FV",
"PG", "TV-PG", "PG-13", "TV-14",
"R", "TV-MA", "NC-17"))|>
  mutate( decade = floor(release_year / 10) * 10)
murder <- netflix_titles|>
  filter(str_detect(description, regex("murder|\\bkill(ed)?\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)))




Show Code
murder|>
  ggplot(aes(y = rating_fct))+
  geom_bar(fill = "#B0CCFF")+
  facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free_x")+
  labs(title = "Netflix Media with Murder", x = "Number", y = "Rating")+
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica Neue")+
theme_light()+
theme(
  text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#263D69")
)+
theme(
  strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#263D69", color = NA),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#FFEBE8")
)











American Comedies by Decade
For this graph, I looked at American comedy movies on Netflix and which decades they were released in. I chose a list of famous comedy actors, including Adam Sandler, Jim Carrey, and Amy Pohler, and used their names to see which movies featured at least one of these actors. I then made a bar graph to compare the number of comedies released in each decade and how many featured someone from my list. I wanted to see whether famous comedy actors appeared more frequently in certain decades and how the number of American comedies changed over time.


Show Code
comedies <- netflix_titles|>
  filter(type == "Movie", str_detect(country, "United States"),
    str_detect(listed_in, "Comedies"))

 
comedies <- comedies |>
  mutate(
    famous_actor = str_detect(
      cast, "\\b(Adam Sandler|Jim Carrey|Will Ferrell|Ben Stiller|Eddie Murphy|Steve Carell|Seth Rogen|Jonah Hill|Paul Rudd|Kevin Hart|Jack Black|Melissa McCarthy|Kristen Wiig|Tina Fey|Amy Poehler|Maya Rudolph|Tiffany Haddish|Jennifer Aniston|Sandra Bullock|Julia Roberts)(?=,|$)"
      ))
    
  
  comedies |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, fill = famous_actor)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#263D69", "FALSE" = "#B0CCFF"),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "No", "TRUE" = "Yes"),
    name = "Contains Famous Comedy Actor"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "American Comedies by Release Year",
    x = "Decade",
    y = "Number of Movies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica Neue")+
theme_light()+
theme(
  text = element_text(size = 9, color = "#263D69")
)











Romantic Comedy
For this graph, I made a data table of all movies that were listed in the categories “Romantic Movies” and “Comedies” to find the romcoms, I then looked in the descriptions of the movie to see which used male pronouns and female pronouns. I also looked at the titles to see which one used some variation of the word love.


Show Code
romcom <- netflix_titles|>
  filter(type == "Movie", str_detect(listed_in, "Comedies"))|>
  filter(str_detect(listed_in, "Romantic Movies"))|>
 mutate(female = str_count(description, regex("\\b(she|her|hers)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
mutate(male = str_count(description, regex("\\b(him|he|his)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)))|>
mutate(love = str_extract(title, regex("\\b(love|lover|loved)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
mutate(love = if_else(!is.na(love), "Love", "No Love"))

  romcom |>
  ggplot(aes(x = male, y = female, color = love)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.5, height = 0.5, size = 2.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#263D69") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Love" = "#263D69", "No Love" = "#B0CCFF"),
    name = "Love in Title"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gendered Pronouns in Romantic Comedies",
    x = "Male Pronouns",
    y = "Female Pronouns"
  ) +
  theme_light(base_family = "Helvetica Neue") +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#263D69")
  )











About the Data
For this project, I used the Netflix Titles dataset from TidyTuesday (April 20, 2021). The original dataset was shared on Kaggle by Shivam Bansal and contains information about movies and TV shows available on Netflix, including their titles, genres, cast members, release years, content ratings, and descriptions.
Source: TidyTuesday Netflix Dataset

title: Candy Data Analysis
text:
Chocolate Candy Performance
For this project, I wanted to look at whether chocolate candies perform better than candies without chocolate. I personally think the best candies contain chocolate and peanuts, so I was interested in seeing whether chocolate was associated with candy popularity. I used the FiveThirtyEight candy dataset, where each row represents a candy and the columns describe its different attributes. The win percentage represents how often a candy was chosen when participants were presented with two candy options.
My null hypothesis is that chocolate content and win percentage are not associated. My alternative hypothesis is that chocolate candies have a higher average win percentage than non-chocolate candies. I will use a permutation test to simulate the null hypothesis and see whether the observed difference is unusual.


Show Code
candy <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/candy-power-ranking/candy-data.csv"
)

candy <- candy |>
  mutate(chocolate = if_else(chocolate == 1, "Yes", "No"))

candy |>
  select(chocolate, winpercent) |>
  head()


# A tibble: 6 × 2
  chocolate winpercent
  <chr>          <dbl>
1 Yes             67.0
2 Yes             67.6
3 No              32.3
4 No              46.1
5 No              52.3
6 Yes             50.3


First, I made a boxplot to compare the win percentages of chocolate and non-chocolate candies. This allows us to see the difference in the distributions before running the simulation. Each group contains candies with a range of win percentages, but I am especially interested in comparing their averages.


Show Code
candy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = chocolate, y = winpercent)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#2A0081", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Chocolate Candy Performance",
    x = "Contains Chocolate",
    y = "Win Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica Neue") +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#2A0081")
  )











Difference in Mean Win Percentage
Next, I calculated the mean win percentage for chocolate and non-chocolate candies. Chocolate candies had an average win percentage of approximately 60.9%, while non-chocolate candies had an average of approximately 42.1%. This gives an observed difference of about 18.8 percentage points. I want to see whether this difference could reasonably occur if chocolate content and win percentage were unrelated.


Show Code
candy |>
  group_by(chocolate) |>
  summarize(mean_win = mean(winpercent))


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  chocolate mean_win
  <chr>        <dbl>
1 No            42.1
2 Yes           60.9


Show Code
observed_diff <- candy |>
  summarize(
    diff = mean(winpercent[chocolate == "Yes"]) -
           mean(winpercent[chocolate == "No"])
  ) |>
  pull(diff)

observed_diff


[1] 18.77927




Permutation Simulation
To test the null hypothesis, I wrote a function called shuffle_test(). This function randomly shuffles the win percentages while keeping the chocolate Yes/No labels the same. It then calculates the average shuffled win percentage for both groups and returns the difference between their means. By shuffling the percentages, I am simulating what the difference could look like if there were no association between chocolate content and win percentage.


Show Code
shuffle_test <- function() {

  shuffled <- candy |>
    mutate(shuffled_percent = sample(winpercent,
                                     size = 85,
                                     replace = FALSE))

  diff <- shuffled |>
    summarize(
      diff = mean(shuffled_percent[chocolate == "Yes"]) -
             mean(shuffled_percent[chocolate == "No"])
    ) |>
    pull(diff)

  return(diff)
}


I then used map_dbl() to run my function 5,000 times. I chose map_dbl() because my function returns one numerical value each time, which is the difference in means from one shuffle. I stored the results in a tibble so I could visualize the distribution of simulated differences.


Show Code
set.seed(123)

simulations <- tibble(
  diff = map_dbl(1:5000, ~ shuffle_test())
)

head(simulations)


# A tibble: 6 × 1
   diff
  <dbl>
1 -6.67
2  7.00
3  1.11
4  3.51
5  2.62
6  6.98




Null Distribution of Candy Popularity
I made a histogram to visualize the 5,000 simulated differences in mean win percentage. The purple bars show the differences that occurred under the null hypothesis, and the pink line represents the observed difference from the original data. The simulated differences should be centered around zero because the null hypothesis assumes that chocolate content and win percentage are unrelated.


Show Code
simulations |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "#2A0081",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_diff,
    color = "#BA1780",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Null Distribution of Candy Win Percentages",
    subtitle = "5,000 Permutations Under the Null Hypothesis",
    x = "Difference in Mean Win Percentage (Yes - No)",
    y = "Number of Simulations",
    caption = "Pink line represents the observed difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica Neue") +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#2A0081")
  )











P-Value and Results
To calculate the p-value, I found the proportion of simulated differences that were greater than or equal to the observed difference. Because my alternative hypothesis is that chocolate candies perform better, I used a right-tailed test. None of my 5,000 simulations produced a difference as large as the observed difference, giving me a simulated p-value of zero. This does not mean the true p-value is exactly zero, but it suggests that the observed difference is extremely unlikely under the null hypothesis.


Show Code
p_value <- simulations |>
  summarize(p = mean(diff >= observed_diff)) |>
  pull(p)

p_value


[1] 0




Conclusion
For this project, I investigated whether chocolate candies have higher average win percentages than non-chocolate candies. I wrote a function to randomly shuffle win percentages and used map_dbl() to repeat the simulation 5,000 times. My observed difference was approximately 18.8 percentage points, and none of my simulations produced a difference as large as the original, giving a simulated p-value of zero (which I report as p < 0.0002). This provides strong evidence of an association between chocolate content and win percentage among these 85 candies, although the data do not establish causation or necessarily represent the preferences of all candy consumers.


About the Data
For this project, I used the Halloween Candy Power Ranking dataset from FiveThirtyEight. The original data came from an online survey in which participants chose their preferred candy in head-to-head matchups. The dataset includes 85 candies and information about their ingredients, characteristics, and win percentages.
Source: FiveThirtyEight Candy Power Ranking Dataset
Original data: Walt Hickey, The Ultimate Halloween Candy Power Ranking, FiveThirtyEight (2017).

title: Taylor Swift - Tidy Tuesday 2
text:
The world has grown up along side Taylor Swift, and with that, her music has changed. Here is a visualization of her songs relationship to loudness and danceability. Each point represents a song and each color represents one of her albums. This data set was made in 2023 so it includes her songs and albums up to that date.

ggplot(Taylor_Swift, aes(x = loudness, y = danceability, color = album_name))+
  geom_point()+
  scale_color_taylor_d() +
  labs(x = "Loudness", y="Danceability", title = "Taylor Swift Danceability", color = "Album")

title: Pixar Movies - Tidy Tuesday 1
text:
Everyone loves a good Pixar movie. You go as a kid, you go as a parent, you go as a college student who misses the innocence and nostalgia that Pixar movies inspire. But why does it feel like every movie is so darn long these days? Let’s explore that through a plot.

pixar_data <- pixar_films |>
  left_join(public_response, by = "film")


ggplot(pixar_data, aes(x = release_date, y = run_time))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x = "Release Date", y="Run Time min", title = "Pixar Films Release Date and Run Times")










Data for this visualization was accessed through the TidyTuesday Pixar Films dataset.
Original data:
Leung, Eric. pixarfilms: An R Data Package to Explore Pixar Films, the People, and Reception Data. Data provided mostly in part by Wikipedia.

title: How Much Does Target Really Know About You?
text:
Companies track our habits to market products to us, but at what point does this become unethical?
In his 2012 New York Times Magazine article, “How Companies Learn Your Secrets,” Charles Duhigg explores how companies use data science and the science of habit formation to influence consumers’ spending habits. At Target, customers are assigned a Guest ID whenever possible, which allows the company to associate their purchases with personal and demographic information. Andrew Pole, a statistician at Target, used data from customers who had created baby registries to identify patterns in their shopping habits throughout their pregnancies. Using this information, he created a predictive model based on approximately 25 products that could estimate whether a customer was pregnant and when she was likely to give birth (Duhigg, 2012). Target could then use these predictions to strategically market products to customers. While impressive, this model and tactic for marketing raises ethical concerns about how much companies should know about their customers and what they should be allowed to do with that information.

title: How Much Does Target Really Know About You?
text:
Companies track our habits to market products to us, but at what point does this become unethical?
In his 2012 New York Times Magazine article, “How Companies Learn Your Secrets,” Charles Duhigg explores how companies use data science and the science of habit formation to influence consumers’ spending habits. At Target, customers are assigned a Guest ID whenever possible, which allows the company to associate their purchases with personal and demographic information. Andrew Pole, a statistician at Target, used data from customers who had created baby registries to identify patterns in their shopping habits throughout their pregnancies. Using this information, he created a predictive model based on approximately 25 products that could estimate whether a customer was pregnant and when she was likely to give birth (Duhigg, 2012). Target could then use these predictions to strategically market products to customers. While impressive, this model and tactic for marketing raises ethical concerns about how much companies should know about their customers and what they should be allowed to do with that information.

title: How Much Does Target Really Know About You?
text:
Ethical Considerations
Using the Data Values and Principles Manifesto, I evaluated four ethical considerations regarding Target’s use of data science.

Principle 1: Use data to improve life for our users, customers, organizations, and communities.
Target’s data model was used to identify potentially pregnant women and provide them with coupons and advertisements for baby-related products. One could argue that this is helpful because it makes pregnant women aware of deals and products they will need for their upcoming birth and child. In her Forbes article, Kashmir Hill (2012) explains that Target also analyzes customers’ coupon usage to determine how large of a discount will incentivize them to purchase a product. While the intention behind these models is primarily to increase sales, customers can also benefit from saving money and receiving more relevant advertisements. I do not think using data for personalized marketing is inherently unethical, but I do think it is important to consider whether the data is being used to benefit the customer or simply to get them to spend more money.


Principle 6: Be open to changing our methods and conclusions in response to new knowledge.
Target did change its marketing methods when it realized that customers were uncomfortable with how much the company knew about them. However, rather than reconsidering whether it was ethical to predict pregnancies without customers’ knowledge, Target changed how it presented its advertisements. According to Duhigg (2012), Target began mixing advertisements for baby products with unrelated products to make the personalized advertisements appear coincidental. From a data science and marketing perspective, Target successfully recognized a problem and adapted its methods. From an ethical perspective, however, I think Target addressed the wrong problem. The problem was not necessarily that customers knew they were being tracked, but that customers were uncomfortable with being tracked to that extent. Rather than addressing their concerns, Target made it more difficult for customers to recognize what was happening.


Principle 10: Respect and invite fair criticism while promoting the identification and open discussion of errors, risks, and unintended consequences of our work.
While most people probably have some idea that companies and apps track their behaviors, I certainly did not know the extent to which this happens and how dedicated companies are to piggybacking on our habits to get us to buy things. I am okay with personalized marketing using my data because I don’t want to be sold a tortoise harness when what I need is a lizard leash. However, I think companies should be more transparent about the extent to which they are invested in our data. Duhigg (2012) explains that Target declined to specify what demographic information it collected or purchased and later disputed his reporting without identifying the specific inaccuracies. How can customers raise concerns about how their data is being used if they do not even know how it is being used in the first place?


Principle 11: Protect the privacy and security of individuals represented in our data.
It seems that Target crosses a boundary when it uses shopping data to identify potentially pregnant women before they have chosen to disclose that information. Duhigg (2012) tells the story of a father who was upset that Target was sending his teenage daughter advertisements for baby products, only to later discover that she was actually pregnant. Regardless of whether Target intended for this to happen, the story demonstrates how personalized marketing can unintentionally expose someone’s private information. Additionally, the customers who created baby registries may not have anticipated that their shopping data would be used to predict other women’s pregnancies. I think there is a significant difference between a company knowing what shampoo I like to use and a company knowing something about my personal life that I have not even told my family. Just because someone provides a company with their shopping data does not necessarily mean they have knowingly consented to all the conclusions that can be drawn from it.


Why Does This Matter?
Ultimately, Target’s use of predictive analytics demonstrates both the impressive capabilities of data science and the ethical concerns that come with them. While customers may benefit from receiving relevant coupons, Target is arguably the biggest beneficiary because it can increase sales and establish long-term relationships with customers. The people whose privacy is compromised, however, may not even know it is happening.
I do not think companies should necessarily stop collecting data or using it to personalize advertisements. However, I think customers should have more knowledge of and control over what their data is being used to predict. There is a difference between using my shopping habits to figure out what products I like and using my shopping habits to figure out intimate details about my life.
Just because data scientists can figure out if someone is pregnant does not mean they should.

title: How Much Does Target Really Know About You?
text:
References
Data Practices. (n.d.). Data values and principles. https://datapractices.org/manifesto/
Duhigg, C. (2012, February 16). How companies learn your secrets. The New York Times Magazine. Read article
Hill, K. (2012, February 24). Target isn’t just predicting pregnancies: ‘Expect more’ savvy data-mining tricks. Forbes. Read article
